title: How regulatory sandboxes help — and where they fall short
label: Regulatory sandboxes · ScaleUp Institute
summary: Irene Graham of the ScaleUp Institute explains how regulatory sandboxes let fintechs test products with realistic data, helping market entry and fundraising. Sandboxes are useful at different stages, but firms worry about cost, duplication with authorisation, and transparency. The FCA’s new scale-up unit and moves to continuous access improve things, but Graham recommends clearer links to authorisation, better sharing of lessons, and faster routes to international markets.

glossary.definition: A controlled environment where firms can test financial products using realistic or live data under regulator oversight.
Financial Conduct Authority, the main UK regulator for financial services and consumer protection.
A dedicated team in the FCA that manages relationships with fast-growing financial firms and helps speed regulatory processes.
Rules that let banks share customer data with other firms, with customer consent, to encourage competition and new services.
A UK government agency that funds and supports innovative businesses across many sectors.
A private company valued at $1 billion or more.
National Health Service — the UK's publicly funded health system.

chapters.title: What the ScaleUp Institute does and why sandboxes matter
chapters.takeaway: Sandboxes let companies test regulated products with realistic data, helping them refine offers and access markets.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please introduce yourself and explain how the ScaleUp Institute engages with regulatory sandboxes.

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: I'm CEO of the ScaleUp Institute. We work across the UK to help companies scale—addressing access to markets, talent, finance and infrastructure—and we advise governments, local authorities and firms.

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: Sandboxes matter because they let fintechs and banks test products using realistic or live data within a regulatory setting so they can refine services and understand regulatory requirements before full market launch.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: When are sandboxes most useful, and when might other regulatory engagement be better?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: They're useful at both start-up and later stages. For new services or partnerships with large banks you want to test in a regulated, data-rich setting. But innovation pathways and other routes can work alongside sandboxes; it isn't either/or.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: Has anyone measured whether sandboxes actually deliver outcomes? The FCA's last big review was in 2017.

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: We track outcomes and can share evidence. Many firms that tested in sandboxes later raised funds or formed partnerships. Not every test succeeds, but successful validation in a sandbox often helped firms attract investment.

chapters.title: Who uses sandboxes and what they gain
chapters.takeaway: Around 200 firms have entered the FCA sandbox; firms use it to validate products, win partners, and signal credibility to investors.

turns.speaker: Lord Hollick
turns.text: Start-ups we heard from said the sandbox duplicates authorisation work and costs them early on. Do you see that?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: Some firms experience duplication and cost, which is valid feedback, but many benefit: testing yields validation that supports fundraising. The experience varies by firm and product.

turns.speaker: Lord Turnbull
turns.text: How many fintechs are there and how many have been through the sandbox?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: About 2,500 fintech firms nationwide. Roughly 200 businesses have entered the FCA sandbox so far; we can provide updated figures and case studies.

turns.speaker: Lord Turnbull
turns.text: Are entrants mainly small start-ups or established companies testing new lines?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: Both. The sandbox serves early-stage firms and established players. It's roughly balanced, maybe skewed toward smaller firms, and firms can use it more than once.

turns.speaker: Lord Lilley
turns.text: Could the apparent benefit you describe be because your members are already later-stage and better placed to use the sandbox?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: Some of our members are later-stage, but benefits are seen across stages. Usage and success depend on firm specifics, so the picture is nuanced.

turns.speaker: Lord Turnbull
turns.text: Can you name sandbox success stories?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: Examples include Zilch and Salary Finance. We can supply more names and evidence of funding or partnerships that followed sandbox participation.

chapters.title: Costs, alternatives and improvements
chapters.takeaway: Firms worry about cost and duplication; improvements include the FCA's scale-up unit, continuous access, clearer links to authorisation, and faster market routes.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bowles of Berkhamsted
turns.text: Are accelerators before or after sandboxes? At what stage should a firm go into a sandbox?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: There’s no fixed order. Accelerators, bank programmes and the sandbox are part of a richer set of options. Firms choose the route that fits their product and readiness.

turns.speaker: Baroness Donaghy
turns.text: You praised the FCA's new scale-up unit and say sandboxes are now open-access rather than cohort-only. How does that help firms?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: Open access removes a timing barrier and the scale-up unit provides account management—direct regulatory contact for fast-growing firms. That should reduce friction and help navigation.

turns.speaker: Baroness Donaghy
turns.text: What remains slow or costly and how fast should it be?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: The slow parts are the links between testing, formal authorisation and getting into procurement or markets. Faster pathways are needed where a product is proven—especially to reach buyers like large banks or public bodies.

turns.speaker: Lord Hill of Oareford
turns.text: Can sandboxes be improved further?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: Yes. Keep them, broaden digital and AI testing, keep improving access, and work internationally to speed market access. The scale-up unit is a helpful recent development.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Fforestfach
turns.text: The US scales faster without sandboxes. Why is that?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: The US advantage is depth of growth capital and large-scale institutional funding. Singapore and others also learned from the UK's sandbox model; market size and capital matter a lot.

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: Also, corporate venturing and acquisitions are more common in the US, which speeds scaling via partnerships and buy‑outs—something the UK could encourage further.

chapters.title: Selection, transparency and next steps
chapters.takeaway: Selection is competitive but open; transparency needs balance between learning and protecting commercial data; the Institute will provide follow-up evidence.

turns.speaker: Lord Davies of Brixton
turns.text: Does the FCA pick winners by choosing cohort members for challenge panels, which could exclude good ideas?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: The challenge route is like any open competition: applicants submit and a selection is made on merit. Firms can reapply or use other routes; having multiple access channels helps avoid unfair exclusion.

turns.speaker: Lord Smith of Kelvin
turns.text: Are sandboxes transparent enough so the wider market benefits from lessons learned?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: There's room to improve. Regulators should publish aggregated lessons while protecting commercially sensitive or personal data. Balancing public insight and competitive confidentiality is key.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You offered to send more evidence on outcomes and successful firms. Anything else you’d add?

turns.speaker: Irene Graham
turns.text: We'll send detailed case studies, funding and partnership outcomes. Also note: some unicorns now use the sandbox even if they didn't scale solely because of it; evidence will show the range of impacts.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you—this has been helpful. We'll expect your follow-up evidence on numbers, success stories and how sandboxes link to authorisation and market access.
